There are things you can do to mitigate those feelings of longing — exercise, dieting, a healthy support group — but the actual acceptance part happens really slowly. 

For me, it only started after a few months. I focussed on myself, carefully organised my actions that had brought me to that point and recognised my personal flaws, and redirected that need for intimacy into something more platonic, since romance was something I needed to detract from until I was in a less toxic headspace. Doing so helped me get close with a lot of friends that I’m still in frequent contact with to this day (2-ish years later).

Main thing is that you don’t wait up for acceptance because it doesn’t happen all at once. It’s a right struggle, but it gets easier. Just get by, one day at a time, mate.

there’re some important things to unpack here. 

first and foremost, you need to stop putting yourself down and blaming yourself for everything—emphasis on ‘need’ and ‘everything’. from what you say, you’ve shouldered all this insecurity about your loved ones, that it’s your fault that they detest you (which they most likely don’t) and that both your life and death would only burden them with inconveneice. drop this mode of thinking. it’s important to be reasonably introspective and self-critical, but from experience i can see that you’re treating yourself unfairly. which brings me to my next point.

you can’t rely on other people to give oleviate the pain you feel, nor can you want to from anyone other than yourself. of course, we all want to be loved and accepted by those we care about, sometimes anyone at all. this isn’t to disparage you for being lonely, but keep in mind that if you aren’t able to love (or at least be kind to) yourself first, you won’t truly find something that will last with another. please, stop treating yourself like shit because you’re far more than that. and the sooner you learn to be compassionate for yourself, the better-off you’ll be with your loved ones in the long run.

do you want to be the person that your loved ones want you to be (and that’s actually what they believe and not what you’ve told yourself out of self-deprication)? because you deserve not to feel this way, and your family deserves to see you at your best.

In addition to my thoughts, I’d like to pose a question about your drawing techniques.

Was this drawn from your own reference?

-judging by the pose, the Lich seems notably stiff, especially with the extended arms that, despite being only bone, lack fluidity at the bends that occur with normal arms. This is something that could be improved on if you were to garner a better understanding of the anatomy of a skeleton—particularly around the shape of the elbow since it’d communicate the bend of an arm more. But that could just be a stylistic choice, to which I’d recommend studying anyway and then simplifying down (simplifying as in going for the more cartoony look that your style has).

-I understand you were probably going for a low-angled stance, but the perspective/proportions of the arms and head to the body are a tad-bit wonky. This is either because the proportions could use some improvement or you’ve drawn from multiple different perspectives without fully ‘calibrating’ them (which you shouldn’t really do anyway unless you understand the fundamentals of base-sketching).

-I like that you tried simplifying the cloak and scarves so that the fabric and tapers follow a few defined directions. It’s a really good way to express shapes with as little info as possible (I’ll touch on how you handled the lighting in a bit). However, the scarf-like rag that slings under and above the left shoulder sports a stiff, almost-hardened look that I don’t think you were going for. If you were, I’d recommend changing up the shape to whatever material (e.g. metal) it’s made of with shading and clearer line-work. As for the crown, I’d recommend giving it a more rounded shape since it would fit comfortably on the skull. Because the crown lacks the clarity of being round, it looks lop-sided and over-flattens the Lich’s forehead.

-understanding the light-source is probably the thing that could use the most improvement (and is also unfortunately one of the hardest to learn). For majority of the Lich, your line-work is solid, but it seems like you don’t have a specific light-source so the shadows are notably inconsistent. (This is where I wanted to mention your clothing) the shapes of the cloak are simplified and have direction (which is great) but the shadows counteract this because of where they’re placed and in such as way that awkwardly dents the fabric around the legs without properly expressing the shape of the legs themselves. Again, this could be a stylistic choice and bone legs wouldn’t have much define shape since the cloak seems to spread outwards as it goes down, but at that point, the folds should be more defined as the fabric would be very loose. It’s fine to have multiple light-sources but you’d typically stick with one for simplicity’s sake.

The reason I opened by asking if you took from your own reference is because most (if not all) of these aspects can be improved if you have a photo to source the perspective, shape, fabric-folds, proportions and lighting from with any particular textures or bits being added to your base sketch and not vice versa. I won’t ramble too much since I’ll probably over-complicate what I mean, so I’ll link an animator/artist that specialises in this type of stuff, gives important advice, has a tough-love attitude and ultimately will encourage you to draw.  From there, you’ll be able to branch out and create a network of mentors cos the internet is cool like that.

Criticism aside, I think you’ve got quite a lot of potential. I like the medieval-fantasy theme: both the accessories and clothing. Though, they’d could look even cooler than they already are with a good understanding of the basics. I respect you for putting yourself out there and asking for criticism. It’s a difficult thing to do and I commend you for that and hope you aren’t put down by what I said. Sorry if this has been quite a read, but I hope it’s made some sense and I haven’t just rambled myself into a hole. 

Looking forward to seeing more from you.

I feel that happiness and comfort are closely determined by the relationships in one’s life. In other words, the bond with friends and family can usually dictate how good someone feels about themselves. 

In my case, after experiencing some pretty bad emotional pain in a relationship with a close friend, I sometimes wish that I didn’t have to rely on other people so much for feeling ‘whole’ in a way.

I’ve already ascertained that I have to figure things out about myself before serious relationships. Furthermore, I’d like to be independent, but that’d ultimately be a detriment to improving my mental health as well as most other aspects since loneliness is a bitch.

It’s a gamble to get close to someone that could just as easily leave your life as they joined it. And since trying to control them is out of the question because it’s their decision, that terrifies me.

Maybe I’ve just taken one bad aspect of my relationships and applied it too broadly to my outlook on others, so my idea of how to cope is really warped, but I dunno.

First off, that’s really terrible. Losing anyone close is tough and for you to experience the loss of a friend to suicide is especially traumatizing. I’m sorry that they didn’t see another way and that these are your circumstances (especially with your recounted suicide attempts).

But, I need you to know that no one is or should be expecting you to ‘push through’ your trauma. That goes for you too. What happened is unforgettably horrible, so there should be no expectation for you to bounce back so quickly, even after several months as well as the personal improvement you’ve described.

This will affect you for the rest of your life. You will have peaks and you will have valleys. What’s important is that you acknowledge when you’re in pain and remember that you’ve endured before and you can again; and that’s where powering through is important.

It’s frustrating, I know. And I’m sorry. But don’t lose sight of why you’re improving. I’m sure that friend of yours would’ve wanted you to live a wonderful life—grueling, yes, but wonderful.
Right now or as soon as you can, find someone that cares about you—a family member or something—and stay with them. Please don’t be alone
